The Rebellion
Fists of the Fallen City
Menu
The mock up
Concept
The main menu presents the player at the edge of a fallen city block at dusk. Menu options are wheatpasted paper posters stuck to a brick wall. It supports the Rebellion tone: grassroots, hand-made, defiant, and still hopeful. It fits the GDD theme (lived-in, human, culturally rich) and palette (mustard yellow, brick red, forest green, warm browns).
Scene layout
Left (about half the screen): brick wall. Red brick with a dark ledge at the base, a boarded door, a fire escape on the building beside it, and green vines along the bottom. The posters and menu sit here.
Right: city street at dusk. A mustard-and-orange sky with a low sun, layered building silhouettes, and a dark street with yellow lane dashes and a streetlamp.
Buildings: Window grids with a few lit in mustard. Rooftops carry a water tank, an antenna, a rooftop hut and vents, with wires strung between them. Ground floors have four shopfronts with striped awnings, one with a sign. A fire escape is drawn on one tower.
Menu elements

[table]
Element | Description
Title | THE REBELLION" in heavy condensed type, cream on a black strip, tilted about 2 degrees. The subtitle "Fists of the Fallen City" sits beneath in mustard monospace.
Fight (selected) | Mustard torn-paper strip, leading ">" marker, straightens and slides right. Starts the game.
Controls | Cream paper strip
Options | Forest-green strip with cream text.
Quit | Warm-brown strip with cream text.
Footer hint | W/S select / Enter confirm", bottom right.
Each option is a separate torn-edge paper strip, tilted slightly. The selected option straightens, moves right and takes the brightest colour. Hover gives the same feedback.
Controls Menu elements(keyboard)
[table]
Action | Primary | Alternate
Move Left/right | A/D | Left or Right arrows keys
Jump | W or Space | Up arrow key board
Light attack | J | Z
Heavy attack | K | X
Special Move | L | C
Pick up | P | N
Parry | T | M
Block | I | V
Options Menu ( elements)

[table]
Settings | functions | Theme | What happens in game
Music volume | Controls the music | a slider. Posters-on-brick feels like it wants a street-ambience bed | Changes the game music level
SFX volume | a slider covering hits sounds parries and dodges | Same theme as the music volume | Change the SFX on or off
Fullscreen | Makes the screen Fullscreen | Same theme as the music volume | Makes the game screen big
Background posters (non-interactive)
"Local Heroes Benefit: Keep the Lights On": cream, forest-green text. Ties back to the original Local Heroes Mural idea.
Rust Notice 114, "CURFEW" struck through: brick red. It shows the Rust security force's control and the community defacing it.
Visual style
Flat shapes with torn, uneven edges (clip-path style); no gradients or glow.
Heavy condensed display type for titles and buttons, monospace for small print.
Palette: brick red #9C3B2E / #7A2F25, mustard #E1A92B, forest green #2F5D3A, warm brown #6B4A2F, cream #E8DCC0, near-black #1D1A16.
Implementation notes (Phaser)

Background as 3 parallax layers: sky and sun, far and near buildings, brick wall foreground. The street strip can be reused as the arena floor backdrop.
Posters and buttons as sprites with irregular alpha edges; a handful of torn-edge shapes can be tinted and reused.
Selection: tween rotation to 0 and x +10px (about 100 ms); swap to the bright colour variant.
Keyboard (W/S, Enter) is primary; mouse hover and click should match.
Placeholder only: the mock up uses stand-in fonts and flat SVG shapes; final art comes from the Art Direction agent.

Game Engine
Phaser
Why Phaser is use for the game building for now.
2D side-scrolling: Phaser is built for 2D and has Arcade physics, sprite animation, and input handling.
Prototype goal: the GDD says Phaser is for "creating a playable prototype". It runs in the browser with no install, so playtesting and sharing a build are easy.
AI-assisted build: the Technical Strategy budgets in tokens, which suggests AI agents write the code. Phaser uses JavaScript or TypeScript, which AI agents oversee well, and it has plenty of documentation and examples.
Small scope: Tier 0 is one character, one enemy type, waves, and a timer. Phaser manages that without much setup.
Theme of the game
Background Themes
Takeaway: Livedin, human, culturally rich.
Corner shops, murals celebrating local heroes, open windows with music drifting out
Basketball courts, food stalls, community gardens
Characters feel connected — casual fits, expressive colours
Colour palette: mustard yellow, brick red, forest green, warm browns
Atmosphere: hopeful, energetic, full of personality and stories
The Story

Character – the hero
Zed — The Boy from BrickRed Alley
Zed grew up in the heart of Fallen City, in a neighbourhood painted with “corner shops, murals celebrating local heroes, open windows with music drifting out” . His block was known for its mustardyellow storefronts, forestgreen basketball courts, and the brickred alley where kids learned to fight, dance, and argue like family. It wasn’t perfect, but it was alive — culturally rich, loud, hopeful, and full of people who looked out for each other.
His mother ran a tiny food stall near the community garden, serving hot bowls of stew to anyone who needed a meal. His father, a muralist, painted the faces of local heroes across the district walls — cooks, musicians, activists, teachers — everyday people who kept Fallen City standing. Zed grew up believing that strength wasn’t about power; it was about protecting the people who gave your life meaning.
The Fall of Fallen City

Everything changed when RUST, the private security force, swept through the districts. The document describes the city as “overtaken Rust a corrupt private Security Force” — and Zed saw it firsthand.
RUST didn’t arrive like soldiers; they arrived like thieves. They shut down the basketball courts. They fenced off the community gardens. They patrolled the alleys where kids used to play. They tore down murals — including his father’s — replacing them with surveillance towers and propaganda screens.
Zed’s father disappeared after confronting RUST officers during a mural teardown. His mother’s food stall was seized for “security violations.” Friends vanished. Neighbours were beaten. The city’s heartbeat went quiet.
Zed didn’t have a choice. He had to fight.
Why Zed Fights
Zed isn’t a soldier. He’s a kid from a livedin neighbourhood who learned to fight the same way he learned to dance — through rhythm, instinct, and community.
His style reflects the game’s pillars:
Impactful, fast-paced combat — Zed’s punches feel like brickred alley brawls, scrappy but sharp.

Skill depth through combos and defence — he learned to juggle, dodge, and parry from street tournaments and late-night sparring behind corner shops.
Wave-clearing under pressure — fighting groups is nothing new; he grew up protecting younger kids from trouble.
He fights not for glory, but to reclaim the places that shaped him — the food stalls, the murals, the music drifting from open windows. The city isn’t just his home; it’s his identity.
Zed’s Personal Mission
Zed’s goal is simple: Take Fallen City back, one district at a time.
Every wave he clears, every arena he survives, every enemy he knocks down brings him closer to finding out what happened to his father — and to restoring the community that raised him.
He fights so kids can play in the basketball courts again. He fights so music can drift from open windows again. He fights so murals can rise again, celebrating real heroes — not corporate tyrants.
Tone & Personality

Zed embodies the game’s theme: “hopeful, energetic, full of personality and stories.” He’s expressive, stubborn, and fiercely loyal. He cracks jokes mid-fight. He refuses to back down. He carries the city’s colours in his outfit — mustard yellow, brick red, forest green — as a reminder of what he’s fighting for.
Character – the Enemy
Enemy Faction Lore: RUST — The Private Security Force of Fallen City
Overview
Rust began as a private security contractor hired to “stabilize” Fallen City after years of political decay and rising crime. But once they were inside, they never left. Rust transformed from a protective force into a militarized occupation, tightening control over every district and crushing resistance with brutal efficiency.
Their name comes from their signature oxidized metal armour, a symbol of decay — a reminder that Fallen City is rotting under their rule.
Rust’s soldiers are not just guards. They are enforcers, hunters, and executioners. Each unit is trained to suppress civilians, eliminate rebels, and maintain absolute control.
⚙️ Rust’s Origin

Rust was founded by Overseer Commander Halden Varr, a former military strategist who believed order could only be achieved through fear. When Fallen City’s government collapsed, Varr seized the opportunity. He offered “protection” to the remaining officials, then quietly replaced them with Rust loyalists.
Within months:
Curfews became mandatory
Districts were sealed
Surveillance drones filled the sky
Anyone who resisted disappeared
Rust became the law. Rust became the city.
🔩 Rust’s Philosophy
Rust operates under a single doctrine:
“Order is strength. Freedom is weakness.”
They believe Fallen City must be rebuilt through force. Civilians are treated as assets to control, not people to protect. Rust’s soldiers are conditioned to see rebels — including Zed — as threats to the “greater good.”

The Rebellion
Fists of the Fallen City
Game Play Systems
Weapon System
Starting in Level 2, weapon boxes are introduced across the levels, giving players access to baseball bats and pipes for combating Grunt enemies
How it works
From Level 2 onwards, Zed can break weapon boxes, pick up baseball bats and pipes using the pickup animation, and carry them using the carrying animation before attacking enemies.
Weapon Rules
Damage: Bats and pipes hit harder than Zed's heavy attack.
Speed and reach: The baseball bat has a quick swing. The pipe has a longer reach but a slower startup.
Durability: Each weapon wears out after a set number of hits. Exact hit counts are listed under Weapon Balance Values.
Breakage: When a weapon runs out of hits it breaks, a short break effect plays, and Zed goes back to using his fists.
Throwing: Zed can throw a carried weapon. A thrown weapon spins through the air and damages the first enemy it hits. Throwing costs durability and the weapon can be picked up again if it survives, see Weapon Balance Values.

Dropping: There is no drop button. Zed drops a carried weapon when he is hit more than 3 times while carrying it, which means the weapon drops on the 4th hit. A dropped weapon lies on the floor and Zed can pick it up again. It keeps its remaining durability. Picking the weapon back up does not reset the hit count.
Attacks with a weapon: Weapons use the existing light and heavy attack buttons. There are no new inputs and no separate weapon move set. The light and heavy mentioned in the core mechanics refer to Zed's light and heavy attacks, not to light and heavy objects.
Weapon types: Only the baseball bat and the pipe exist for now. There are no other weapons or upgraded versions.
Weapon boxes: Each level from Level 2 has one weapon box in a fixed placement. The box holds one weapon, either a baseball bat or a pipe. Which weapon it holds is fixed for each level and is chosen by the level designer. It is not random. Boxes do not respawn.
Enemy use: Weapons are for Zed only. Enemies cannot pick up or use weapons.

HUD: While Zed carries a weapon, the HUD shows a small icon of that weapon with its remaining durability next to the health bar.
Weapon Balance Values
Reference: Starting values, tuned against Zed's current moves (light hits 6, 7 and 12 damage, heavy attack 18 damage with a 12 frame startup) and a Grunt's 30 HP. Frames are at 60 per second. These are first-pass numbers and can be retuned in playtesting.
Baseball bat: Damage 20. Startup 7 frames, active 4, recovery 16. Reach is a hitbox 64 wide. Knockback 400. Hitstun 26 frames. Durability 10 hits. A Grunt goes down in 2 hits.
Pipe: Damage 24. Startup 12 frames, active 4, recovery 20. Reach is a hitbox 84 wide, the longest in the game. Knockback 360. Hitstun 28 frames. Durability 8 hits. A Grunt goes down in 2 hits.

Light and heavy buttons: The light button swings the weapon at the values above. The heavy button does the same swing with 25 percent more damage and 25 percent more knockback, and costs 2 durability instead of 1. The heavy swing deals 25 damage with the bat and 30 damage with the pipe. A heavy swing still goes through when the weapon has only 1 durability left, and the weapon breaks afterwards.
Thrown weapon: Damage 15, knockback 300, hitstun 20 frames. It travels at 480 pixels per second for up to 320 pixels and hits the first enemy in its path. A throw costs 2 durability, the same as a heavy swing. If the weapon still has durability left after the throw, it lands on the floor where it hit an enemy or at the end of its flight, and Zed can pick it up and keep using it until its durability runs out. If the weapon has 2 durability or less when thrown, the throw still goes through and the weapon breaks when it lands, with the same break effect as a worn-out weapon.
Weapon box: A weapon box breaks after 2 hits from Zed. The box break animation is added separately.

chunks.heading: Zed Special Attack: Rage System
chunks.text:
The Rebellion: Game Design Document section. Final draft for review.
Status: design complete. Numbers are starting values to be tuned in playtests. See Section 10 for open items.

chunks.heading: 1. Design Intent
chunks.text: Level 1 is the pace level. The player learns movement, the light and heavy chain, jump kick and block with no extra pressure. From Level 2 onward, a Rage meter rewards aggressive, clean play and builds toward a short, powerful state in which Zed unleashes his Special move.

chunks.heading: 2. Lore
chunks.text:
Zed's rage is born from the Rust's false promises, the disappearance of his father, and his willingness to fight for his city.
The Special is the release of that rage: a refusal to let his city fall the way his father was taken from it. The Rust is the source of the rage, so every Rust enemy feeds it. The father's story stays implied in the Special itself and is left for cutscenes and dialogue to reveal.

chunks.heading: 3. Availability
chunks.text:
[table]
Level | Rage meter | Special
Level 1 (pace level) | Hidden, cannot fill | Unavailable
Level 2 onward | Visible and active | Available when the meter is full
The meter resets to 0 at the start of every level and on a retry. Nothing carries over.
On Level 2 the meter slides into the HUD and a one-time prompt explains it.

chunks.heading: 4.1 Source
chunks.text:
Landing a blow on any Rust enemy, including bosses, adds Rage.
Every blow adds the same base amount, whichever normal move lands it (light, heavy or jump kick).
All of Zed's normal moves work as usual until the meter is full.
Misses give nothing. Kills and combo finishers give no extra bonus.

chunks.heading: 4.2 Clean-streak bonus
chunks.text: Landing blows without taking a hit in between adds a bonus. Taking a hit ends the streak.

chunks.heading: 4.3 Drain
chunks.text:
The meter drains on a timer at all times, whether or not the player is fighting. The drain pauses during the pause menu, wave transitions and any cutscenes.
[table]
Setting | Value
Meter range | 0 to 100
Base gain per blow | +3
Clean-streak bonus | +2 extra per blow after 3 consecutive clean blows (so +5)
Streak resets when | Zed takes a hit
Drain while building | 2 per second

chunks.heading: 5. Ready State
chunks.text:
When the meter reaches 100, Rage is READY. It holds at 100 for a 4-second window so the player can finish what they are doing and press L. If the window passes without the press, the meter starts draining from 100 on the normal timer and must be rebuilt.
The window exists because a full meter that drained at once would fall below 100 and could never fire.

chunks.heading: 6.1 Activation
chunks.text:
With the meter READY, the player presses L (keyboard). The gamepad binding is to be designed.
If Zed cannot start Rage at that moment (for example, mid-jump), the press is buffered and Rage begins when he lands.
A hit or a knockout cancels a buffered press. The press is also lost if the READY window runs out first.

chunks.heading: 6.2 During Rage
chunks.text:
Rage lasts 9 seconds, with the meter draining about 11 per second on a fixed clock. Nothing speeds it up or slows it down: not hits landed, not kills, not damage taken.
Zed's normal attacks are replaced by one Special move. It does not add to them.
Zed can still move, jump and block. There is no dodge during Rage.
The meter gains no Rage during Rage, and kills during Rage give nothing.
The Special does strong damage but never a full boss kill. The player must still finish a boss with normal attacks.

chunks.heading: 6.3 Ending
chunks.text: Rage ends when the meter reaches 0, or immediately if Zed is knocked out (health reaches 0). A knockdown from a hit does not end it. Zed's normal moves then return, and the meter must be refilled from 0 by landing blows on Rust enemies.

chunks.heading: 7. Expected Pacing
chunks.text:
Assuming about 1.2 blows per second in active combat:
[table]
Play style | Time to fill
Sloppy (frequently hit, little bonus) | About 60 seconds
Clean (long no-hit streaks) | About 25 seconds
Not fighting | Meter drains to 0 in about 50 seconds
The target is one or two Rages per level for most players. Clean play is visibly faster, but sloppy play is never locked out.

chunks.heading: 8. Art Direction
chunks.text:
For the Art Director. A rage meter that visibly fills from Level 2 onward, placed near Zed's health bar but clearly distinct from it in shape and colour.
Palette: ember to orange to red-white as it fills.
Motion: the meter bubbles or pulses, and the pulse gets faster as the fill rises.
READY state: the frame flares, a READY cue and the L prompt appear, and a visible 4-second window shows how long the player has.
Rage active: the meter shows a clear 9-second countdown.
Zed: a subtle aura while building, and a stronger glow on his eyes and fists for the whole of Rage. The art can hint at the loss behind it, with grief turning to fire.
Feedback: spark or number pops at the meter on each blow, a flash and impact beat on activation, and a distinct effect when Rage ends.
Accessibility: do not rely on colour alone. Use pulse speed and icon changes as well.

chunks.heading: 9. Implementation Notes
chunks.text:
Treat special as a named input action, bound to L on keyboard, so the gamepad binding can be added later without changing the state machine.
Keep all tuning numbers (gain, bonus, streak length, drain, READY window, Rage duration) in one config.
Rage needs a state in the player state machine that swaps the attack set for the single Special move and disables dodge.
The meter system listens for blows landed, hits taken, knockout, level start, retry, pause and wave transition.

chunks.text:

Item | Status
Special move damage and recovery time | Placeholders. Set during balancing. Per-hit damage and the 9-second duration must be balanced together so the Special is strong but never a full boss kill.

chunks.heading: Assumptions to confirm at sign-off
chunks.text:
The 4-second READY window (added so a draining full meter can still be used).
The starting numbers: +3 per blow, +2 bonus after 3 clean blows, drain of 2 per second, Rage duration of 9 seconds.
A heavy attack and a jump kick give the same Rage as a light attack.
A knockdown does not end Rage. Only a knockout does.
A hit cancels a buffered L press.
The meter resets on a retry as well as at level start.
Lore wording has not yet been checked against the existing GDD and content/lore files.

Q1 | Special is triggered by L. The gamepad binding comes later.
Q2 | One single move.
Q3 | Lore as in Section 2.
Q4 | Rage resets each level.
Q5 | The meter drains, including when full. Rage is a timed state in which the Special replaces normal attacks.
Q6 | Kills during Rage give nothing. The meter is built by landing blows on Rust enemies.

chunks.heading: The Rebellion: Fists of the Fallen City — AI Dev Pipeline
chunks.text:
A complete map of the AI-driven development pipeline used to take the GDD to a playable 2D browser brawler (Phaser 3, 8 levels), what it produced, what is still manual, and what it costs.
> **Evidence note.** Everything below was audited from this repository on 2026-11-03 (files, git history, blackboard log, playtest reports, and a fresh `npm test` run: **163 tests, 163 pass, 0 fail**). Where the repo holds no evidence, this document says so rather than guessing. That matters most in section 4 (cost).
---

chunks.heading: 0. The pipeline at a glance
chunks.text:
```
GDD (6 .docx + 2 PDF, human-written)
 │
 ├─ A. CONTENT PIPELINE pipeline/*.mjs (ingest → brief → generate → validate/repair → report)
 │ 4 writer agents: lore · enemies · levels · dialogue → content/*.json + content/build/content.json
 │
 ├─ B. DESIGN AGENTS .claude/agents/ (art-direction, ux-flow, menu-ui, music, 8 level-style agents,
 │ critic, refiner) → design/*.md, assets/*.svg, content/levels/styles/*.json
 │
 ├─ C. BLACKBOARD (goal-oriented build loop) blackboard/
 │ G1 read-gdd ┐
 │ ├→ G3 find-gaps → G4 prioritise → G5 generate-code → G6 review ─(fail)→ G5
 │ G2 scan-code┘ (owner approves each gap)
 │
 ├─ D. GAME BUILD src/ (Phaser 3.80.1, ~10.6k lines of non-test JS) + index.html
 │
 └─ E. PLAYTEST AGENTS qa/playtest-agents/ G7 levels · G8 bosses (Playwright, real key presses, video, invariants)
 → blackboard/facts/playtest-*.json → rebalance → re-run
```
33 agent definitions live in `.claude/agents/`. Two agents never talk to each other: the blackboard (`goals.json`, `facts/`, `log.md`) is the only channel, and `board.mjs` is the only writer of goal state.

chunks.heading: 0. The pipeline at a glance
chunks.text:
| Stage | Entry point | Model calls? |
|---|---|---|
| Ingest + brief + validate + report | `npm run content` | No (free, deterministic) |
| Writer agents | `npm run content:generate` (spawns `claude -p`) | Yes |
| Blackboard round | "use blackboard-director-agent to run the goal board" | Yes |
| Tests | `npm test` | No |
| Playtests | `npm run playtest` / `:levels` / `:bosses` | No (scripted agents, not LLM calls) |
| Play it | `python dev-server.py 8777` → `index.html` | No |
---

chunks.heading: 1. What did the pipeline produce?
chunks.text: Counts below are from `content/REPORT.md` (2026-10-28), `content/build/content.json` (built 2026-11-02), and file listings. "In the build" means the playable game reads or plays it; "generated only" means it exists as data but the game does not use it yet.

chunks.heading: Story and dialogue
chunks.text:
| Item | Count | In the playable build? |
|---|---|---|
| Lore entries | 67 (17 proposed, 50 canon) | **Partly.** The story intro card (`src/ui/storyData.js`) is lifted from `content/lore/` (GAP-027, owner-approved). Districts 2–8 lore feeds level styling. |
| Enemy entries | 22 | **Yes** for the units that have stats/sprites (grunt, Watcher, Breaker, Copper Fang, Brick Dugan, Railgun Royce). Others are stat blocks only. |
| Level definitions | 8 (41 waves total: 5/5/5/6/7/4/3/6) | **Yes.** `src/levels/levelData.js` loads `content/levels/levels.json` + `rust-gdd-levels.json` + 8 style files. |
| Dialogue entries | 99 (87 proposed) | **Only title-screen copy (7) and options-menu copy (22).** I found no runtime reference to the Zed barks (fight-start, combo, heavy-hit, low-HP, block, wave-clear, win, lose, retry), Rust taunts, or neighbour lines. That is ~70 entries generated but not wired. |
| Rage HUD copy | local file | Yes (`src/ui/rageHudCopy.js`) — hand-wired, not from the dialogue pipeline |

chunks.heading: Story and dialogue
chunks.text: Validation: 57 of 57 source documents ingested, **0 schema/canon errors** across all four content types. **113 items are marked `proposed` and are awaiting owner approval** (`content/REPORT.md`).

chunks.heading: Art assets
chunks.text:
- **4,097 pixel-art PNG frames** under `assets/sprites/` — Zed (1,048), Brick Dugan (873), Railgun Royce (419), Rust Breakers (504 + 375 Type 2 + 72 walking + 80 action), Rust Watchers (375), Copper Fangs (128), hit/death FX (89 + 80), items such as bat, boxes and health pickups (54). Metadata (`assets/sprites/metadata.json`) shows they were produced with a pixel-art character/animation generator (the design docs name Pixel Lab) using text prompts and an 8-direction template.
- **Vector (SVG) UI and menu art:** 14 UI pieces (bars, buttons, panel, icons, victory card frame), 11 menu layers/posters, 8 level backgrounds, FX placeholder.
- **Still placeholders (15 SVGs in `assets/sprites/`):** drone, elite drone, megadrone, hologram, Iron Line cordon, Overseers Calder / Holt / Voss / Wren, Halden Varr, plus the original grunt/Watcher/Breaker/Copper Fang/Zed placeholders.

chunks.heading: Audio (31 files in `assets/sound/`)
chunks.text: 8 level tracks, 2 boss tracks, menu theme, results music, level-complete sting, and ~16 SFX (punches, kicks, grunts, death cries, footsteps, whoosh, "go"). Music was sourced by `music-agent` from CC0 libraries (`design/audio/audio-manifest.md`). **Licence gap:** the SFX filenames are Freesound IDs and the repo records no licence or attribution for them (`design/audio/CREDITS.md` covers music only).

chunks.heading: Gameplay systems (all covered by `npm test`, 163 passing)
chunks.text: Light/heavy/finisher combat, parry with indicator, dodge/block, jump and kick, grab/throw, weapon pickups (bat, pipe), Zed's Rage system with HUD and entry flash, wave spawner with `ambush` / `pincer` / `surge` patterns, crew-waits-for-leader logic, boss health bar, bespoke boss AI for Brick Dugan (charge, grab, mega stomp, wall slam, rage punch, block) and Railgun Royce, title screen, main menu with parallax, options panel, pause, mute, victory card, loading screen, story card.

chunks.heading: Quality evidence from the playtest agents
chunks.text:
- First full pass (2026-11-02): 22 runs, **0 invariant failures** (no soft-locks, bound leaks, stuck grabs, frozen timers, missing result screens or JS errors, including fuzzing and edge-abusing personas).
- Findings it raised: Level 1 finale was too punishing (Brawler lost 3 of 4); Level 5's 210 s timer too tight; only Dugan was a real boss (others were stand-in grunts).
- After the crowd-control and Level 1 rebalance, Level 1 full runs went **won 4/4** and the finale **won 4/4** for the competent personas. One new issue was logged (Dugan charging for 3 minutes without being hit by the "Rookie" persona).
- Honest caveat from the reports themselves: 3–4 runs per row, enemy AI unseeded — direction, not proof.
---

chunks.heading: 2. What manual steps remain?
chunks.text:
| # | Manual friction point | Where it shows up |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Owner approval of 113 "proposed" items** (lore, enemies, all 8 levels, 87 dialogue). Nothing generated is canon until you say so. | `content/REPORT.md` |
| 2 | **Wiring generated content into the game.** Dialogue/barks and most lore are data only; a person or a code agent must hand-wire each one (e.g. `rageHudCopy.js` is still hand-written). | `src/`, `content/dialogue/` |
| 3 | **Art is made outside the pipeline.** Sprites are generated in an external tool, exported by hand, dropped into folders with ad-hoc names (some contain curly quotes and em dashes), then registered by hand in `assets/asset-keys.json` and `design/art/asset-manifest.md`. | `assets/sprites/` |
| 4 | **Remaining stand-in enemies and bosses.** Holt, Wren, Copper Fang (as end boss), Varr and several Rust units still spawn as grunts with an HP multiplier (`STAND_IN` in `levelData.js`); 15 placeholder SVGs remain. | `src/levels/levelData.js` |
| 5 | **Audio sourcing and licence checks.** The agent could not open OpenGameArt (HTTP 403); picks were not listened to; a human downloads, auditions and approves. SFX licences are unrecorded. | `design/audio/` |
| 6 | **Each blackboard round is human-triggered and human-steered.** You `reset`, ask the director to run, then pick which gap to build and approve it. (This is a deliberate gate, but it is manual.) | `blackboard/log.md` |
| 7 | **Playtest needs a real browser.** On 2026-11-03 G7 was blocked: the cloud sandbox had no Chromium and the Playwright CDN was blocked. Runs only work on your machine today. | `blackboard/log.md` |
| 8 | **Test list is hand-maintained.** `package.json` enumerates ~50 test files by name; a new test file is silently skipped until someone adds it. | `package.json` |
| 9 | **Duplicated data to keep in sync.** Level data lives in `content/levels/*.json` and a fallback mirror in `src/waves/waveData.js`. | `src/waves/` |
| 10 | **Human judgement of "feel".** Reports repeatedly flag questions only a human can answer (does the wave-3 hint teach? is Dugan's charge fair?). | `qa/playtest-agents/runs/*/SUMMARY.md` |
| 11 | **Housekeeping and delivery.** 9 modified + 3 untracked paths are uncommitted; a 19 MB `_playtest_bundle.tar.gz` and `_to_delete/` are manual leftovers; GDD source typos ("Rush" for "Rust") must be fixed by the document owner. | repo root |
| 12 | **Cost is not metered anywhere** (see section 4). | — |

chunks.heading: 3. What would it take to eliminate them?
chunks.text: Full automation is possible for most of this; a few steps are deliberately human and should be replaced by *policy*, not removed.

chunks.heading: 3. What would it take to eliminate them?
chunks.text:
| Manual step | What 100% automation requires |
|---|---|
| 1. Approval of proposals | Replace per-item review with a **rule-based auto-approver**: auto-accept `proposed` items that pass the critic agent, cite sources, and conflict with no canon; escalate only conflicts. Record approvals in the blackboard. (Removes the gate for low-risk copy; keep a human for story-changing items.) |
| 2. Wiring content into the game | A **content-binding layer**: a generated manifest (`trigger → content id`) and a runtime `Barks.play(trigger)` that reads `content/build/content.json`. Add a gap-analyst check "every dialogue trigger has a call site", so G3 finds and G5 builds unwired content automatically. |
| 3. External art | Call the art generator from a **scripted step** via its API (prompt → generate → download → slice → name → register in `asset-keys.json`), driven by `asset-manifest.md`. Add a CI check that every manifest entry has a file and every file has a key. Needs an API key and a credit budget cap. |
| 4. Stand-ins and placeholders | Make the same art step **consume the enemy roster** (22 entries) so each unit gets sprites; add a G-goal "no `STAND_IN` waves allowed" that blocks release until bosses have bespoke AI and sprites. |
| 5. Audio | Pin audio to **licence-verified sources with an API** (Freesound/Kenney/OGA mirrors), have the agent record licence + URL per file into `CREDITS.md`, and fail CI on any file lacking a record. Auditioning by ear can be replaced by loudness/loop-point analysis plus a spot check. |
| 6. Human-driven rounds | A **scheduled runner** (CI or scheduled task) that runs `reset → director → review` nightly and opens a PR per gap; owner approval becomes PR review. |
| 7. Browser playtest | Run playtests in **CI with the Playwright image** (Chromium preinstalled, `--renderer canvas`), upload videos and `report.json` as build artifacts, and feed failures back into G5 automatically. |
| 8. Test list | Use `node --test "src/**/*.test.*"` so tests are discovered, not listed. |
| 9. Duplicate data | Delete the mirror; load `content/build/content.json` as the single source and generate the fallback at build time. |
| 10. Feel | Not automatable. Replace with a **small scheduled human playtest** (5 players, recorded) and use telemetry from the same invariants the agents track (time-to-clear, HP at finale, deaths per wave). |
| 11. Housekeeping | Pre-commit hook + CI: run tests, block uncommitted generated output, auto-clean temp bundles. GDD typo fixes: let the critic agent open an edit request to the document owner. |
| 12. Cost metering | Run every headless agent with `claude -p --output-format json`, append `total_cost_usd` and token counts to `pipeline/cost-log.jsonl`, and have `run.mjs` and `board.mjs` print a per-stage total. About 20 lines of code. |

chunks.heading: 3. What would it take to eliminate them?
chunks.text:
**Realistic ceiling:** items 2, 6–9, 11 and 12 can be fully automated with code. Items 3–5 can be automated given paid APIs and a spend cap. Items 1 and 10 stay human by design, reduced to review and playtest rather than hand-work.
---

chunks.heading: 4.1 Total actual run cost
chunks.text:
**$ not recorded — the repository contains no usage, billing, token or cost data, so I cannot state an actual dollar figure without inventing one.**
I searched every pipeline script, the blackboard, the playtest runner and the settings file for cost, token, usage and credit tracking. The only hits were unrelated words. `pipeline/run.mjs` calls `claude -p` and prints the exit code and last lines of output, but discards token counts and cost. Blackboard log entries carry timestamps but no usage.
What *can* be stated from evidence:

chunks.heading: 4.1 Total actual run cost
chunks.text:
| Component | Cost evidence |
|---|---|
| Ingest, brief, validate, report (`npm run content`) | $0 — no model calls |
| Tests (163) and the scripted playtest agents | $0 — local code, no LLM calls |
| Music | $0 — CC0 sources, no attribution required for the picks that shipped |
| Sound effects | Licence/cost not recorded (verify) |
| Writer agents, blackboard agents, design agents, code generation | **Unmetered.** They ran through the Claude Code CLI; cost depends on your plan (subscription usage vs. API billing), and no per-run figure was captured |
| 4,097 pixel-art frames | **Unmetered.** Generator credits/subscription not recorded in the repo |
| Human time | Not tracked (84 commits across 2026-10-04 → 2026-11-03) |
**To get the real number (takes a few minutes):**

chunks.heading: 4.1 Total actual run cost
chunks.text:
1. On the machine where the agents ran, run `npx ccusage` (reads Claude Code's local session logs) and filter to 2026-10-04 → 2026-11-03 for this project. That gives actual tokens and API-equivalent cost per day and per session.
2. Open the art generator's billing/usage page and read credits spent on the Zed, Dugan, Royce, Breaker, Watcher and Copper Fang batches.
3. Paste both totals in here:
| Line item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Claude Code usage (writer + blackboard + design + code agents), 2026-10-04 → 2026-11-03 | $____ |
| Art generator credits | $____ |
| Audio / other | $0 (CC0) + $____ |
| **Total actual run cost** | **$____** |
If you share the `ccusage` output or billing exports, I will fill this table in from them.

chunks.heading: 4.2 Most expensive pipeline step
chunks.text:
**Not measurable from this repo.** Based on structure only (this is an inference from token volume, not a measurement):
- **Likeliest top model-spend step: the writer agents with full-document briefs** (`npm run content:generate`). Each of the four writers receives a RAG brief plus whole primary documents (`fullDocs` in `pipeline/config.mjs`, e.g. all of "The Rebellion.docx", the 18-chunk Rage spec) and runs a repair loop up to `--repair N` rounds, with the level and dialogue writers also reading lore and enemy output. Output was large (99 dialogue entries, 67 lore entries).
- **Second: blackboard G5 code generation and G6 review**, repeated per gap across 6+ rounds (logs show 4–6 gap builds on 2026-10-13, 10-19), each re-reading `contracts.md`, the diff and the full test run.
- **Likely largest *non-LLM* spend: the sprite generator** — 4,097 frames is far more volume than any text step.
The cost-log step in section 3 (row 12) turns this guess into a measured answer after one run.

chunks.heading: 4.3 Solo / small-team sustainability
chunks.text:
**Assessment: very likely sustainable for a solo developer or small team, with two conditions.** This is a judgement from the pipeline's structure, not from a measured bill.
Why it is sustainable:
- **The expensive part is bounded and one-off per change.** The deterministic stages (ingest, validate, test, scripted playtests) are free, so cost scales with how often you regenerate content or build a gap, not with every run.
- **Each blackboard round is small.** The log shows individual agent tasks finishing in roughly 1–2 minutes, one gap per round, so cost is incremental and controllable.
- **Free-licensed audio and a free engine** (Phaser, CC0 music) keep fixed costs near zero.
- **Quality gates catch waste early.** 0 validation errors on the final run, tests and invariant-checking playtest agents mean fewer paid retries.
Conditions that must hold:

chunks.heading: 4.3 Solo / small-team sustainability
chunks.text:
1. **Meter it.** Without a cost log you cannot know whether a full regeneration costs a coffee or a week of budget. Do section 3, row 12 before scaling up.
2. **Cap art generation.** Sprites are the volume risk; set a credit budget per character and reuse rigs. Re-generating all ~4,100 frames when one design changes would be the most expensive mistake available.
Main risk to sustainability is not API spend but **human review time** (113 proposals, wiring, art cleanup, feel playtests); automating items 2, 6, 7 and 9 in section 3 reduces that most.
---

chunks.text: set up the blackboard that runs the Shared workspace for the goal-oriented agents. Agents never message each other. They read the board, claim a goal they own, post a fact, and mark the goal done.

chunks.heading: Blackboard
chunks.text:
Shared workspace for the goal-oriented agents. Agents never message each other. They read the board, claim a goal they own, post a fact, and mark the goal done.
```
blackboard/
 goals.json goals, owners, preconditions (needs), status, attempts
 facts/ what agents have published (one file per goal)
 log.md append-only history
 board.mjs the only thing that edits goals.json
```

chunks.heading: Goal chain
chunks.text:
```
G1 read-gdd ----\
 >-- G3 find-gaps -- G4 prioritise -- G5 generate-code -- G6 review
G2 scan-code ---/ ^ |
 +---- fail --------+
```
| Goal | Agent | Reads | Publishes |
|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | `gdd-reader-agent` | `pipeline/corpus/`, GDD docs | `facts/gdd-requirements.json` |
| G2 | `code-scanner-agent` | `src/`, tests, `assets/asset-keys.json` | `facts/code-inventory.json` |
| G3 | `gap-analyst-agent` | G1 + G2 facts | `facts/gaps.json` |
| G4 | `prioritiser-agent` | `facts/gaps.json` | `facts/priorities.json` |
| G5 | `code-generator-agent` | `facts/priorities.json`, `design/team/contracts.md` | code in `src/`, `facts/generated.json` |
| G6 | `reviewer-agent` | `facts/generated.json`, the diff, `npm test` | `facts/review.json` |
| G7 | `playtest-level-agent` | `playtest.html`, `qa/playtest-agents/` (plays levels 1-8 on video) | `facts/playtest-levels.json` |
| G8 | `playtest-boss-agent` | `playtest.html`, `qa/playtest-agents/` (plays mini-bosses + end bosses on video) | `facts/playtest-bosses.json` |

chunks.heading: Goal chain
chunks.text: G1 and G2 are independent, so run them in parallel. A failed review reopens G5, which resets G6 (`board.mjs reopen`). After `maxAttempts` the goal becomes `blocked` and the director reports it to the owner.

chunks.heading: Commands
chunks.text:
```bash
node blackboard/board.mjs status
node blackboard/board.mjs ready
node blackboard/board.mjs claim <goal-id>
node blackboard/board.mjs done <goal-id> "note"
node blackboard/board.mjs block <goal-id> "reason"
node blackboard/board.mjs reopen <goal-id> "reason"
node blackboard/board.mjs reset
```

chunks.heading: Run it
chunks.text: Ask Claude Code: **"use blackboard-director-agent to run the goal board"**. It loops: `ready`, spawn the owners (in parallel when several are ready), repeat, until nothing is open. To run another round on the next gap, `reset` then run again; G1/G2 will refresh the facts.

chunks.heading: Playtest agents (G7, G8)
chunks.text:
Goal-oriented, adversarial AI players that press real keys, record video and check invariants every frame (soft-locks, bound leaks, frozen timer, stuck grabs, JS errors). They need nothing upstream, so run them any time, or after G6 to check a change in play. Details: `qa/playtest-agents/README.md`.
```bash
node qa/playtest-agents/run.mjs --suite levels # G7
node qa/playtest-agents/run.mjs --suite bosses # G8
```

chunks.heading: Rules every agent follows
chunks.text:
1. Claim before working (`claim`). If the claim fails, stop: someone else has it or the needs are unmet.
2. Write only your own `facts/` file, and only the code your goal allows.
3. Every fact carries evidence: a chunk id (`the-rebellion#8`) or `file:line`. No evidence, mark it `suspected`.
4. Missing input? `block` the goal with the reason. Never guess.
5. Need something new? Add it to the `requests` array of your fact file for the director to turn into a goal.
6. Never edit `GameDesignDocument/` or `goals.json`.

chunks.heading: Boss health bar (art and feedback spec)
chunks.text:
Status: PROPOSED starting values for playtest. Owner: art-direction-agent. Covers the big end-of-level health bar shown in the HUD while a boss ("Brick" Dugan first) is alive. Feedback and layout only: no gameplay number changes (150 HP, 0.30 rage threshold, hitstun immunity, hit-stop and everything in `duganData.js` are fixed inputs). Flat vector, everything drawn with Phaser Graphics and Text in `HudScene`, no new image files, fonts are the existing `FONTS.button` (Anton) and `FONTS.body` (Rubik). Times are ms from the named event; px are 1280x720 view pixels.
Builds on: `hit-feedback-spec.md` section 7 (enemy bar: border, bevel, bands, delayed drain chunk, KO behaviour), `dugan-wall-slam.md` and `dugan-grab-break-cue.md` (structure, Reduced Motion, Hit Flash Low), `style-guide.md` section 2 (Rust palette, combat signal colours) and `design/ux/hud.md` (HUD clutter rules).

chunks.heading: 1. Intent
chunks.text:
Dugan is the player's first real skill check. Until now he wears the same 96x10 bar as a grunt, so nothing says "this one is different". The boss bar fixes that with three reads, in order: (1) a heavy riveted Rust steel frame with a hazard-stripe cap and a name plate announces a big fight, (2) a long cyan fill with a bright leading edge and a cream chunk that drains after each hit shows exactly how much each blow cost, (3) a notch, a skull and a hatched "danger zone" at the left end tell the player that the last 30 percent is a different fight (Rage Punch). Then it pays off: the notch is crossed, the bar goes hot, the name plate rattles, and the plate stays tense until he drops and the bar shatters.
Faction look: Rust, not Hope. Steel, soot (Rust Ink), Gunmetal, hazard orange stripes, Visor Cyan for healthy fill (same cyan as every Rust enemy bar, so the player already reads cyan as "enemy health"), brick-red hatching for the danger zone. No Mustard, no Cream plate (Cream appears only as text and as the damage chunk, exactly as on the enemy bar).

chunks.heading: 1. Intent
chunks.text: Readability rules: HUD scene only, so the bar never gets covered by sprites. Single near-white area is the 40 px leading-edge flash for 66 ms (rate limited, section 6.4). The frame never rotates or tilts (style guide: never rotate HUD text). Colour is never the only signal (section 11).

chunks.heading: 2.1 Where, and why
chunks.text: Block anchor: top-centre, x 320 to 960 (640 wide, centred on x 640), y 138 to 230. Existing HUD (from `HudScene.js`): ZED label and health bar x 32 to 392 / y 20 to 80; Rage meter x 32 to 342 / y 96 to 118 (Level 2+); wave block centre x 640 / y 20 to 84; LEVEL name text centre x 640 / y 100 to 124; timer and score top-right x 1048 to 1248 / y 20 to 96; boost readout top-right y 100 to 136; wave banner centre x 640 / y 240 (88 px, about y 195 to 285); GO arrow right y 360; pause hint bottom-right y 676 for 5 s.

chunks.heading: 2.1 Where, and why
chunks.text:
Why top-centre under the level name and not the bottom:
- The play lane is y 460 to 680 (`LANE`), and fighters' feet go all the way to y 680. A bottom bar (even a thin one at y 684 to 716) would sit under the front-lane feet, collide with the pause hint and with Zed's lowest shadow, and the player's eyes (on Zed and the boss) are in the middle of the screen. Top-centre keeps the boss bar where the enemy's name and health are read without leaving the action.
- The top-centre column is the one place that is empty from y 124 down to the banner: the wave block ends at about y 84, the level name ends at y 124. Left (Zed bar, Rage meter) and right (timer, score, boost) stay untouched, and the bar's width stops at x 320 and x 960, so it is clear of the Rage meter (right edge about 342) by its y range (118 vs 138) and of the boost text (x 1048+).
- Dugan is 192 px tall. At the far lane (feet y 460) his head reaches about y 268, 38 px below the bottom of the bar block (y 230). Grunts are shorter. A high jump can briefly overlap the bar region; the HUD draws above the world, and the bar is opaque, so it stays legible.
- It is where players of the genre already look for an end-level boss bar (top-centre).

Fill Rust Ink #14181C, 3 px Steel #7C8A96 border, bottom edge flush with the frame top (y 168). Two 2.5 px rivets (Steel Light #A9B6C1) at (x+9, y+15) and (x+w-18, y+15) |
